subject: Measurements of the visionary temple's gates, walls, and chambers

figures.name: Thickness of the wall of the building (40:5)
figures.note: Both MT and LXX give 6 cubits (long cubit); SP does not contain Ezekiel.

figures.name: Length of the threshold of the gate (40:6)
figures.note: MT repeats 'one reed broad' (likely dittography); LXX has only one occurrence, suggesting MT corruption.

figures.name: Length of the vestibule of the gate (40:8-9)
figures.note: MT 40:8 contains a verse absent in LXX (likely a doublet of v.9); LXX preserves the shorter, probably original text.

figures.name: Length of side chamber (40:7, gate guard rooms)
Total length of the gate (40:15)
figures.note: MT reads 50 cubits but the sum of components (6+6+5+6+5+6+6+8+2 etc.) yields 50 in MT and is contested; LXX gives a different reckoning, reflecting divergent architectural reconstructions.

figures.name: Length of the inner court gate (40:21)
Distance from inner gate to outer gate (40:23, 27)
Width of side rooms by north gate (40:48)
figures.note: MT gives '5 cubits on this side and 5 on that'; LXX adds '14 cubits broad' for the gate width which MT lacks (LXX preserves a numerical detail likely lost in MT haplography).

figures.name: Length of vestibule of the temple (40:49)
Width of vestibule (40:49)
figures.note: MT 'eleven' (עשתי עשרה) vs. LXX 'twelve' (δώδεκα); a classic scribal confusion involving similar Hebrew numeric forms or a deliberate symmetry adjustment.

figures.name: Steps up to the vestibule (40:49)
figures.note: MT lacks a number; LXX reads 'ten steps' (δέκα ἀναβαθμοῖς), likely preserving an original detail dropped in MT or assimilating to symbolic numerology.

systematic_analysis.pattern: The divergences in Ezekiel 40 are not systematic in the sense of the Genesis 5/11 chronologies (no consistent +100 or ×2 rule). Rather, they cluster around (a) doublets and pluses in MT (e.g., 40:8), (b) small numeric variations likely from graphic confusion (11/12, presence/absence of 'ten steps'), and (c) divergent reckonings of summed gate measurements. The Samaritan Pentateuch is irrelevant here since Ezekiel falls outside the Pentateuch.
systematic_analysis.pattern_plain: Unlike the patriarchal ages, the differences in Ezekiel 40 don't follow a single mathematical rule. They look more like scattered scribal slips, expansions, and architectural reinterpretations than a coordinated revision.

theories.name: Independent transmission of architectural data
theories.summary: MT and LXX-Ezekiel descend from divergent Hebrew Vorlagen, with LXX-Ezekiel (especially Papyrus 967) attesting a shorter and sometimes differently-numbered text. The temple-vision measurements were transmitted in parallel streams, each making sense of an inherently complex architectural description differently.
theories.summary_plain: The Hebrew and Greek versions of Ezekiel come from different ancient editions of the book, so their numbers don't always match. Each tradition tried to make the temple's complicated layout add up in its own way.
supporting_evidence: Papyrus 967 (LXX) shows a markedly different recension of Ezekiel with distinct chapter order and numerous quantitative variants.
LXX-Ezekiel is roughly 4–5% shorter than MT-Ezekiel, suggesting genuine textual plurality, not mere translation choices.
Lust, Tov, and Crane have demonstrated that LXX-Ezekiel translates a shorter Hebrew Vorlage faithfully.
The 'ten steps' in 40:49 LXX matches the architectural logic of the inner gates' graded ascent, suggesting independent preservation.
weaknesses: Some variants (like the missing 'ten steps' in MT) could be simple haplography rather than separate editions.
Distinguishing Vorlage variants from translator harmonization is methodologically difficult.

theories.name: Scribal error in numeric forms
theories.summary: Many of the small divergences (11 vs 12 cubits, presence/absence of 'ten', dittography in 40:6, the doublet at 40:8) are best explained by ordinary copying errors: graphic confusion of Hebrew numeric spellings, parablepsis, and dittography. These do not constitute a coordinated pattern.
theories.summary_plain: Most of the differences look like ordinary copying mistakes — a number written twice, a phrase accidentally skipped, or two similar number-words confused.
supporting_evidence: MT 40:8 is widely regarded as a vertical dittograph of 40:9 and is absent in LXX.
Hebrew numeric expressions are notoriously prone to graphic confusion (e.g., עשתי עשרה vs. שתים עשרה).
The 'one reed' phrase in 40:6 is repeated in MT but single in LXX, a classic dittography signature.
Such errors are sporadic, matching the unsystematic distribution of divergences.
weaknesses: Scribal error cannot account for larger structural differences such as the divergent total gate length.
Some 'errors' may instead be deliberate harmonizations to architectural totals.

theories.name: Theological/symbolic motivation
theories.summary: A minority view holds that some numeric variants reflect deliberate adjustment to symbolic ideals (e.g., perfecting symmetry to multiples of 5 or 10, or matching Solomon's temple in 1 Kings 6). The 'ten steps' and 11→12 shift could reflect such tendencies.
theories.summary_plain: Some scholars suggest that ancient editors tweaked numbers to make the temple's measurements more symbolic or symmetrical.
supporting_evidence: 12 cubits vs. 11 produces a more symbolically resonant number (twelve tribes, etc.).
Ten steps fits a graduated sacred ascent pattern echoed elsewhere in temple ideology.
Ezekiel's vision is itself a theologized architectural program, inviting later symbolic refinement.
weaknesses: Most variants do not move toward obviously 'better' symbolic numbers.
There is no consistent ideological direction across the chapter.
The evidence is equally compatible with accidental error or independent Vorlagen.

theories.name: MT expansion (pseudo-deflation inverse)
theories.summary: In Ezekiel, the typical pattern (when one tradition is fuller) is that MT has pluses absent in LXX — the inverse of the Genesis chronology debate. The 40:8 plus and the dittographic 'one reed' in MT suggest expansionist tendencies in the proto-MT tradition of Ezekiel.
theories.summary_plain: In the book of Ezekiel, the Hebrew text often has extra material the Greek lacks — the opposite situation from Genesis. Some scholars think the Hebrew tradition added detail over time.
supporting_evidence: LXX-Ezekiel is consistently shorter; Tov estimates ~4–5% less text.
Several MT pluses in chapter 40 have telltale doublet features.
Qumran fragments (4QEz) sometimes side with the shorter LXX text.
weaknesses: Not all MT pluses are expansions; some LXX minuses reflect translator condensation.
The slug 'mt_deflation' is awkwardly applied here since MT is the longer text in Ezekiel.

overall_assessment: The numerical divergences in Ezekiel 40 are best explained by a combination of independent textual traditions (LXX translating a genuinely shorter Hebrew Vorlage attested at Qumran and in Papyrus 967) and ordinary scribal error in the transmission of numeric forms. Unlike the patriarchal chronologies of Genesis 5 and 11, no systematic mathematical rule governs the differences; the pattern is sporadic, consisting of dittographies, haplographies, and small numeric confusions, with occasional larger reckoning differences in summed measurements. The Samaritan Pentateuch is not a witness here, since Ezekiel lies outside the Pentateuch. These data confirm that Ezekiel circulated in two distinct editions in the Second Temple period, and that proto-MT Ezekiel underwent modest expansion relative to the Vorlage of LXX.
overall_plain: The number differences in Ezekiel 40 don't follow a neat formula like the ages of the patriarchs do. They mostly reflect two slightly different ancient editions of Ezekiel plus normal copying mistakes, with the Hebrew version often slightly longer than the Greek.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Two editions of Ezekiel, no master formula
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most significant implication is that Ezekiel — like Jeremiah — circulated in two parallel editions during the Second Temple period, and the architectural numbers of chapter 40 are a sensitive probe of that pluriformity. Unlike the Genesis chronologies, where coordinated patterns betray ideological revision, Ezekiel 40's variants show the messier reality of how numerical data drift through independent transmission.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The differences here show that Ezekiel existed in two slightly different ancient editions, and that even sacred temple measurements weren't immune to the normal slippage of hand-copied texts.

_validation.confidence_note: The general framework (two editions of Ezekiel, sporadic variants) is sound, but several specific numerical claims and LXX readings appear inaccurate or unverifiable.

flagged_claims.claim: Total length of the gate (40:15) ... mt_value: 50, lxx_value: 25
flagged_claims.reason: The claim that LXX gives 25 cubits for the total gate length in 40:15 is not a standard textual datum; LXX-Ezekiel 40:15 is textually difficult but the specific value '25' here appears fabricated or unsupported.

flagged_claims.claim: LXX adds '14 cubits broad' for the gate width which MT lacks
flagged_claims.reason: This specific LXX plus of '14 cubits' at 40:48 is not a standard textual datum; the MT here actually has a known plus regarding gate breadth (often reconstructed as 14 cubits from LXX), but the figure and direction of the variant are stated imprecisely.

flagged_claims.claim: Steps up to the vestibule (40:49) ... LXX reads 'ten steps' (δέκα ἀναβαθμοῖς)
flagged_claims.reason: LXX 40:49 does have a number of steps that MT lacks, but the standard LXX reading is typically 'ten steps' in some witnesses while others read differently; presenting it as a fixed δέκα reading oversimplifies the witness tradition.

flagged_claims.claim: Width of vestibule (40:49) ... MT 'eleven' vs. LXX 'twelve'
flagged_claims.reason: This variant is real but the explanation invokes 'similar Hebrew numeric forms' — עשתי עשרה vs שתים עשרה are not especially graphically similar, weakening the proposed scribal mechanism.

flagged_claims.claim: Qumran fragments (4QEz) sometimes side with the shorter LXX text
flagged_claims.reason: The Qumran Ezekiel fragments (4QEzek-a/b/c, 11QEzek) are very fragmentary and do not clearly attest to chapter 40 measurements; the claim that they 'side with the shorter LXX' overstates what these scraps demonstrate.

flagged_claims.claim: Lust, Tov, and Crane have demonstrated that LXX-Ezekiel translates a shorter Hebrew Vorlage faithfully
flagged_claims.reason: While Lust and Tov are real scholars who argue this, 'Crane' is less standardly cited in this triad; the specific attribution should be verified.

flagged_claims.claim: LXX-Ezekiel is roughly 4–5% shorter than MT-Ezekiel
flagged_claims.reason: Tov's commonly cited figure for LXX-Ezekiel's shorter text is closer to 4–5% but is sometimes given differently; precise percentage should be verified against Tov's actual statement.

flagged_claims.claim: MT 40:8 is widely regarded as a vertical dittograph of 40:9 and is absent in LXX
flagged_claims.reason: While 40:8 is indeed often considered a doublet and is shorter/absent in LXX, characterizing this as a 'widely regarded' consensus is somewhat overstated.

safe_claims: The Samaritan Pentateuch is irrelevant here since Ezekiel falls outside the Pentateuch
Papyrus 967 (LXX) shows a markedly different recension of Ezekiel with distinct chapter order
LXX-Ezekiel is shorter than MT-Ezekiel overall
Ezekiel circulated in two distinct editions in the Second Temple period (parallel to Jeremiah)
The divergences in Ezekiel 40 do not follow a systematic mathematical rule like Genesis 5/11
Hebrew numeric expressions are prone to graphic/scribal confusion in transmission
